title: Before writing a new scenario test, check for existing tests covering the same code path
content: When planning scenario test tasks, enumerate the distinct code paths to be covered and assign at most one test file per distinct path. If two scenarios exercise the same guard clause branch with only superficial differences (different file names, scenario name strings), merge them into a single parameterized test rather than creating separate files. Flag any planned test that appears to duplicate an existing test's code path as a merge candidate.
rationale: Duplicate test files add maintenance burden and review noise without improving coverage. The machine review flagged ~800 lines of redundant test code across four separate findings. Test deduplication at planning time is cheaper than cleanup at review time.

title: When adding a new terminal state to a decision FSM, immediately enumerate all write paths and add guards to each
content: When adding a new terminal state to an existing FSM: (1) grep for all functions that call SaveDecision/SaveDecisions or check decision.Action, (2) list each as a subtask, (3) add guards to all of them in the same implementation cycle. Do not consider the terminal state 'implemented' until all write paths are guarded.
rationale: Terminal state bugs are asymmetric: the happy path works, but re-decision attempts corrupt state silently until a specific test exercises that exact combination. Enumerating all paths upfront prevents the multi-cycle repair pattern that occurred here.

title: Before implementing a new hash or ID computation, grep for existing implementations of the same algorithm
content: When a spec or task description says 'using the same algorithm as X', that is a directive to call X's function, not to re-implement it. Before implementing any hash, ID, or normalization function, grep for existing implementations. If the spec says 'same as Y', make the planner task explicitly reference reusing Y's implementation.
rationale: Duplicated algorithms diverge silently over time. The spec's own language ('same algorithm as materialization IDs') was a clear signal that was ignored, resulting in a duplication that the review flagged but did not fix due to pre-existing status.

title: Always sort display lists by timestamp fields, never by ID strings
content: When planning tasks that involve sorting or ordering items by recency, always use the actual timestamp field (CreatedAt, UpdatedAt, etc.) as the sort key. Never use string IDs as a proxy for temporal ordering — IDs may not be monotonic strings, may include prefixes, or may be generated by systems with different ordering semantics. Verify that the sort key is a time.Time in any PR that adds or modifies list display functions.
rationale: This class of bug is subtle in tests because test data is often created sequentially with IDs that happen to sort correctly lexicographically. The bug only manifests in production when runs have IDs that do not sort lexicographically in chronological order. A heuristic makes this a planning-time check rather than a review-time catch.

title: Before planning implementation, verify every acceptance criterion is independently testable — defer if any criterion is placeholder or purely abstract
content: When planning implementation for a spec, enumerate all acceptance criteria and check each one for testability: can a pass/fail determination be made from observable output alone? If any criterion is a placeholder (e.g., 'Criterion 1'), copy of the criterion title, or purely abstract (no observable behavior specified), halt planning and request criterion refinement. Do not begin task breakdown until every criterion maps to at least one automated or manually verifiable check. Flag the spec as 'needs-refinement' rather than continuing with unverifiable criteria.
rationale: The test-spec run showed that a spec with a placeholder criterion ('Criterion 1') completed validation with 0 automated checks but scored 1 passed acceptance criterion — a false positive that inflates trust signals. Placeholder criteria cannot be validated automatically, so they silently pass through the acceptance scorer while producing no real coverage. Catching this at planning time prevents implementation work from proceeding against a spec that cannot be verified.

title: When a product review shows all behaviors as 'unclear', treat the spec as requiring revision before planning the next implementation cycle
content: After any run where the product review records every behavior card with automatic_status 'unclear', do not plan another implementation cycle against the same spec. Instead: (1) review whether the acceptance criteria are concrete and observable, (2) determine whether the scenario test infrastructure is exercising the right code paths, (3) revise the spec or scenario tests before re-entering planning. 'Unclear' at the scenario level means the pipeline cannot confirm any behavior automatically — additional implementation cycles accumulate work without building trust. Flag the spec for revision and block further decomposition until at least one behavior transitions to 'passed'.
rationale: The test-spec run (run-1a65fbac308ba37c) produced a product review with 1 behavior at 'unclear' status and 0/0 criteria confirmed. A second iteration against the same spec would repeat this outcome since no structural change was made. The planner must treat an all-unclear product review as a spec quality signal, not an implementation shortfall.

title: Before queuing a run against a spec, verify the spec has been revised since its last do_not_accept_without_changes posture
content: Before scheduling any implementation run against a spec: (1) look up the most recent prior run for that spec, (2) check its process review recommended_posture, (3) if posture was 'do_not_accept_without_changes', verify that the spec file has been modified since that run's timestamp. If the spec is unmodified, block the run and surface the posture warning — do not silently re-execute. A spec that has not changed cannot produce a different outcome. This check must happen at queue time, not post-run.
rationale: my-spec completed three consecutive runs (run-aac415fba8d44e42, run-1a65fbac308ba37c, run-072a517edf3b4c1f) with identical structural failures: 0 automated checks, all behaviors unclear, recommended_posture do_not_accept_without_changes each time. Prior proposals addressed single-run reactions but contained no pre-run gate. Without a gate, the pipeline will re-execute indefinitely against a structurally broken spec, accumulating accepted outcomes that carry no real verification signal.

title: Boundary-detection tests must place the subject fixture exclusively on one side of the boundary
content: When writing a test that verifies a section or range boundary (e.g., 'content after heading X is excluded'), the file or value under test must appear ONLY on the side being tested, not in both regions. If the fixture appears both inside the target region AND beyond the boundary, the test passes regardless of whether boundary detection works — it is not a boundary test, it is a positive-match test. To test exclusion: (1) ensure the subject appears only after the boundary, (2) assert false/empty, (3) verify the test fails if you remove the boundary logic. For inclusion tests, ensure the subject appears only inside the target region.
rationale: In 0004h-remediation, a test for '## heading boundary stops AC section scan' placed main_test.go in both the AC section and the Scenarios section, then asserted want:true. This passed whether or not the boundary was detected, providing zero signal that the boundary logic worked. The machine review flagged this across multiple findings. The heuristic makes this a planning-time check on test design rather than a review-time catch.

title: Regression tests for string-search bugs must use the exact trigger string from the original bug
content: When writing a regression test for a bug that was triggered by a specific string pattern (e.g., a function matched 'Acceptance Criteria' instead of '## Acceptance Criteria'), the prose in the test must contain the exact triggering string — including casing, punctuation, and context — that the old code would have matched incorrectly. If the test prose uses a variant that the old code would NOT have matched (e.g., lowercase 'acceptance criteria' when the bug triggered on capitalized 'Acceptance Criteria'), old code and new code produce identical results and the test does not serve as a regression guard. Before finalizing any regression test: verify that the test case would FAIL against the buggy implementation.
rationale: In 0004h-remediation, the specACMentionsPath regression tests placed only lowercase 'acceptance criteria' in prose sections before the real ## heading. The original bug searched for capitalized 'Acceptance Criteria' using case-sensitive strings.Index. Lowercase prose would not have triggered the old bug, so all prose-mention test cases were vacuous — they passed with both old and new code. The machine review identified this across multiple findings. This heuristic makes string-casing fidelity a planning-time check when writing regression tests.

title: Proof checks for 'confirm prior fix' tasks must inspect current file state, not diff presence
content:
When a task's objective is to confirm that a prior cycle's fix is still in place — or to verify that a file has been deleted — proof checks must use direct filesystem or code inspection: `grep -q 'pattern' file`, `test ! -f path`, `go test -run TestName`. Never use diff-based evidence (examining git diff output, looking for the change in the diff) to confirm a fix is present. A fix applied in cycle N will NOT appear in the diff when assessed in cycle N+2, making it appear absent even when correctly in place. This causes the runner to generate redundant fix tasks that re-verify already-correct state, cycling indefinitely.

Specifically:
- For 'delete file X' tasks: proof check is `test ! -f X`, not diff inspection
- For 'change string S to T in file F' tasks: proof check is `grep -q 'T' F`, not diff inspection
- For structural confirmations: grep, go test, or direct file reads are authoritative; diff presence is not
rationale: In 0004h-remediation (run-f183a076113ff186), the specACMentionsPath fix was implemented in cycle 2 (t-003) but triggered 20+ redundant confirmation tasks over 10 cycles because the acceptor examined diff evidence and found the change absent. Similarly, 'delete duplicate test file' tasks (t-005, t-006, t-011, t-012, t-015, t-016, t-019, t-020...) were repeated 8+ times each because diff-based assessment saw no deletion event (it had already occurred in a prior cycle). Direct state checks — grep for expected content, test for file absence — break the thrash cycle. The review outcome confirmed this was the sole cause of 10-cycle thrashing: 'reviewer hallucinating a fixed bug on an out-of-diff file — not a code problem.'

title: Nil-guard tests must exercise both branches: guard-fires and guard-does-not-fire
content:
When writing a test for a nil-guard pattern (`if obj != nil { obj.Method() }`), create sub-tests or table entries for both branches: (1) guard fires — the guarded operation is skipped, the surrounding logic still produces correct results; (2) guard does not fire — the guarded operation executes, the operation completes normally. If the test only exercises the branch where the guard fires (skips the call), a regression that adds an unconditional call on the second branch will cause a nil-dereference panic that the test cannot catch.

Concretely for event-log nil guards:
- Sub-test 1: nil eventLog + condition that triggers guard → verify correct result, no panic
- Sub-test 2: nil eventLog + condition that does NOT trigger guard → verify correct result, no panic
rationale: In 0004h-remediation, the nil-eventLog unit test (AC 14) only exercised the guard-fires path where the spec AC mentions the original file and the correction is rejected. The complementary path — where the guard does not fire and a correction is accepted — was untested with nil eventLog. If an unconditional eventLog.Append were accidentally added to the accepted branch, a nil-dereference panic would go undetected. The machine review flagged this across code_quality, logic_gaps, spec_alignment, and test_coverage facets. Testing both branches at planning time prevents this asymmetry.

title: t.Fatal and t.FailNow must not be called inside goroutines spawned by the code under test
rationale: In 0004l (run-f84b6611b397f9f3), TestScenario_ReviewStage_FileUnreadable_FailSafeRetainsFinding used a neverCalledInvoker whose Invoke called n.t.Fatal from inside a goroutine spawned by VerifyBlockingFindings. If the verifier were incorrectly reached, the goroutine would exit without sending to resultsChan, causing VerifyBlockingFindings to deadlock waiting for goroutineCount results. The test would hang rather than fail, making the defect undetectable. Five review facets flagged this as a warning. The pattern of 'assert never-called by panicking inside the goroutine' is a common Go testing mistake.

title: When a spec defines a verbatim LLM prompt template, proof checks must verify that all named field substitutions are present in the implementation
content:
When a spec defines an LLM prompt template with named field substitutions (e.g., `Finding: [severity] [file]:[line] — [description]`), the implementation task must include at least one proof check that greps for each named field in the prompt-building code. A field named in the spec template must appear as a variable reference in the prompt format string.

Concretely, if the spec template contains `[severity]`, `[file]`, `[line]`, and `[description]`, proof checks must include:
  grep -q 'f.Severity' <prompt-building-file>
  grep -q 'f.Description' <prompt-building-file>
  grep -q 'f.File' <prompt-building-file>
  grep -q 'f.Line' <prompt-building-file>

A comment like '// minimal implementation' or '// simplified prompt' in the prompt-building code is a strong signal that the template was not fully followed. Treat this as a proof check failure.

The corresponding test for the LLM invoker must assert that the prompt content includes the required fields (e.g., strings.Contains(prompt, f.Description)), not merely that the invoker was called. A test that only checks invoker.calledWithPrompt != "" provides no evidence that the prompt contains the right information.
rationale: In 0004l (run-f84b6611b397f9f3), LLMFindingVerifier.Verify built its prompt with a comment '// Build prompt (minimal implementation)' and omitted f.Severity and f.Description from the template. The spec defined the template explicitly as 'Finding: [severity] [file]:[line] — [description]'. The test TestLLMFindingVerifier_ReadsFileContextCorrectly only checked invoker.calledWithPrompt != "" — it could not detect missing fields. Five review facets flagged the prompt deviation as a warning. Without proof checks that grep for the field names, this class of spec-template deviation passes all automated gates.

title: File-path membership tests must include a same-basename collision case
content:
When implementing a function that classifies findings or items by file-path set membership (e.g., 'is this file in the diff?'), the test suite must include a case where two different files share the same basename (e.g., internal/foo/util.go and internal/bar/util.go are both in the diff, and a finding references internal/baz/util.go). The test must assert that the finding is NOT treated as in-set, confirming that full-path matching is used, not basename iteration.

Without this test, an implementation that iterates all set members and compares basename values will pass all other tests (since most tests use unique filenames) while silently bypassing verification for any finding whose basename collides with a diff file. This is the exact failure mode that the verifier was designed to prevent — a finding that should be verified gets skipped because its file appears to be 'in the diff'.

This applies to: diffFiles maps, allowlists, blocklists, and any predicate over a set of file paths.
rationale: In 0004l (run-f84b6611b397f9f3), isInDiffFiles iterated all diffFiles keys and compared filepath.Base values. If internal/foo/util.go was in the diff, any finding with File: internal/bar/util.go would be incorrectly classified as in-diff and bypass verification. The spec was designed precisely to prevent false positives where a reviewer hallucinates a bug on an untouched file. Basename collision re-introduces that failure mode silently. Five review facets flagged this as a warning. The absence of a collision test allowed the flawed implementation to pass all acceptance criteria.

title: Goroutine fan-out must use a channel buffered to the fan-out count
rationale: In 0004l (run-f84b6611b397f9f3), VerifyBlockingFindings spawned goroutineCount goroutines sending to an unbuffered resultsChan. If verifier.Verify panicked inside any goroutine, that goroutine exited without sending, and the collection loop blocked forever. Five review facets flagged this across architecture_drift, code_quality, logic_gaps, spec_alignment, and test_coverage. The fix is structural — buffering the channel means a panicking goroutine can still send (or a recover can send a fail-safe result) without blocking the collector.

title: Switch on an interface-sourced enum type must include a default fail-safe case
content:
Any switch statement over a value whose type is defined in an interface (e.g., a disposition string returned by a FindingVerifier interface method) must include a `default` case that:
1. Logs or surfaces the unexpected value (e.g., log.Printf("unexpected disposition %q", d))
2. Fails safe — retains the item, returns an error, or otherwise avoids silent data loss

Rationale for the rule boundary:
- Internal constants (iota, unexported string constants within a single package): a default case may be intentionally absent if all values are exhaustively listed and the compiler will catch new additions.
- Interface-sourced values: any implementation can return any value, including zero-value ("") and future additions. No compiler check enforces exhaustiveness. A missing default silently drops data.

The zero-value case is especially dangerous: if a FindingVerifier returns (VerifierResult{}, nil) — an empty struct, nil error — the switch receives Disposition="" (zero value), skips all known cases, and silently applies the behavior of the absent default, which in Go is a no-op. The finding is lost with no log, no event, no audit entry.

Example anti-pattern:
  switch result.Disposition {
  case DispositionConfirmed:
      kept = append(kept, result.Finding)
  case DispositionFixed:
      // suppress
  case DispositionDowngraded:
      result.Finding.Severity = SeverityWarning
      kept = append(kept, result.Finding)
  // zero-value Disposition silently reaches here and drops the finding
  }

Example correct pattern:
  switch result.Disposition {
  case DispositionConfirmed:
      kept = append(kept, result.Finding)
  case DispositionFixed:
      // suppress
  case DispositionDowngraded:
      result.Finding.Severity = SeverityWarning
      kept = append(kept, result.Finding)
  default:
      log.Printf("unexpected verifier disposition %q for %s:%d — retaining finding", result.Disposition, result.Finding.File, result.Finding.Line)
      kept = append(kept, result.Finding) // fail safe
  }
rationale: In 0004l (run-f84b6611b397f9f3), the disposition switch in VerifyBlockingFindings had no default case. A FindingVerifier implementation returning VerifierResult{} with nil error would produce Disposition="", which falls through all cases silently — the finding is dropped with no log, no event, and no audit entry. This is identical behavior to DispositionFixed but unintentional and invisible. Five review facets flagged this across architecture_drift, code_quality, logic_gaps, spec_alignment, and test_coverage. The interface contract cannot guarantee all callers return valid dispositions.

title: Wiring tasks for large infrastructure files must specify the exact function name and insertion anchor
content:
When a task involves wiring a new component into an existing Go source file larger than 200 LOC (e.g., a stage provider, router, or dependency injection file), the task objective must include:
1. The exact function name to modify (not just the file path)
2. The existing code pattern that marks the insertion point (e.g., 'after the line that creates reviewAdapter' or 'inside the `if p.claudeProvider != nil` block, after reviewRunner construction')
3. Any prerequisite struct field names or config literal patterns where the new field must appear

Without this context, the executor must reverse-engineer the correct insertion point from a large file, which frequently fails in complex wiring files where multiple similar construction patterns exist.

Task objective anti-pattern:
  'Wire LLMFindingVerifier into RealStageProvider.BuildStages in cmd/gromit-next/stage_provider.go. Inside the p.claudeProvider != nil block...'

Task objective correct pattern:
  'Wire LLMFindingVerifier into RealStageProvider.BuildStages in cmd/gromit-next/stage_provider.go. Read the file first. Find the ReviewStageConfig literal (search for `ReviewStageConfig{`). Add Verifier: and WorkDir: fields. Add the verifierAdapter construction immediately after the reviewAdapter construction in the `if p.claudeProvider != nil` block. The NewFallbackAdapter call should use tier "low" and the same costCallback/invocationCallback variables already present in that block.'

This rule triggers when: the target file has more than one construction site for similar types, the spec describes the insertion as 'inside block X after Y', or the task has failed once already on the same wiring objective.
rationale: In 0004l (run-f84b6611b397f9f3), task t-008 (wiring LLMFindingVerifier into stage_provider.go) failed in 2 consecutive attempts. The task objective described what to do but not where — the executor had to infer the insertion point from a 400+ LOC file with multiple construction patterns. Both attempts failed proof checks. Providing the function name, insertion anchor, and field names up front would have made the task deterministic. This is a distinct failure mode from task t-023 (mockInvoker definition) which failed due to conflicting mock definitions in the same package.

title: In-place mutation of a finding's fields must propagate to all collections containing that finding
rationale: In 0004l (run-f84b6611b397f9f3), VerifyBlockingFindings downgraded a finding from SeverityError to SeverityWarning and correctly removed it from result.BlockingFindings. However, result.AllFindings still held the original Error-severity copy. ReviewResultEvent computed findingsBySeverity from result.AllFindings, producing a payload with blocking_findings=0 but findings_by_severity.error=1. Three review facets (architecture_drift, code_quality, logic_gaps) flagged this as a warning. The contradiction would mislead any downstream consumer cross-checking these fields.

title: strings.Split on file content must trim the trailing empty element before indexing
content:
When parsing file content line by line using `strings.Split(content, "\n")`, always trim the trailing empty element before any indexing or slicing:

  lines := strings.Split(content, "\n")
  if len(lines) > 0 && lines[len(lines)-1] == "" {
      lines = lines[:len(lines)-1]
  }

Alternatively, use `strings.TrimRight(content, "\n")` before splitting:

  lines := strings.Split(strings.TrimRight(content, "\n"), "\n")

Why this is always required: virtually all Go source files (and most text files) end with a newline character. `strings.Split("a\nb\n", "\n")` returns `["a", "b", ""]` — three elements, not two. Without trimming:
- `len(lines)` is one greater than the actual line count
- Range-based end clamping (`min(endLine, len(lines))`) includes the spurious empty element in excerpts
- Display strings like `fmt.Sprintf("lines %d to %d", start, len(lines))` overcounts the line range by 1
- The excerpt sent to an LLM prompt claims to show lines N to M+1 when the file has only M real lines

This is the common case, not an edge case. Code that omits this trim will be subtly wrong for virtually every real input.
rationale: In 0004l (run-f84b6611b397f9f3), LLMFindingVerifier.Verify split file content with strings.Split(content, "\n") without trimming the trailing element. The endLine clamping used len(lines) as the upper bound, so lines[startLine:endLine] always included a spurious empty trailing string in the excerpt. The verifier prompt told the LLM it was showing 'lines N to M+1' when the file had only M real lines. Four review facets (architecture_drift, code_quality, logic_gaps, spec_alignment, test_coverage) independently flagged this as a warning, each noting 'nearly all Go source files end with \n, making this the common case.'

title: All fail-safe return paths within a feature must use a consistent reason-string suffix
content:
When a function has multiple fail-safe return paths — paths where an error condition is handled by returning a safe default rather than propagating — all of those paths must use the same suffix in their reason strings. This enables audit log consumers and operators to pattern-match on fail-safe events without enumerating individual reason strings.

Establish the pattern on the first fail-safe path added to a function and apply it consistently to all subsequent paths:

Anti-pattern (inconsistent suffixes):
  // file read fails
  return VerifierResult{Disposition: DispositionConfirmed, Reason: "file unreadable — retaining finding"}, nil
  // invoke fails
  return VerifierResult{Disposition: DispositionConfirmed, Reason: "invoke error — retaining finding"}, nil
  // parse fails (missing suffix)
  return VerifierResult{Disposition: DispositionConfirmed, Reason: "parse error"}, nil

Correct pattern (consistent suffix):
  return VerifierResult{Disposition: DispositionConfirmed, Reason: "file unreadable — retaining finding"}, nil
  return VerifierResult{Disposition: DispositionConfirmed, Reason: "invoke error — retaining finding"}, nil
  return VerifierResult{Disposition: DispositionConfirmed, Reason: "parse error — retaining finding"}, nil

With the consistent suffix, a single grep or log filter (`grep 'retaining finding'`) surfaces all fail-safe activations across all error types. Without it, consumers must know every possible reason string to detect systematic verifier failures.

This rule applies to any feature that has 2+ fail-safe paths — verifiers, adapters, retry handlers, and similar components where detecting the activation pattern is operationally important.
rationale: In 0004l (run-f84b6611b397f9f3), LLMFindingVerifier.Verify had three fail-safe paths: 'file unreadable — retaining finding', 'invoke error — retaining finding', and bare 'parse error'. The parse-error path was missing the '— retaining finding' suffix. Four review facets (architecture_drift, code_quality, logic_gaps, spec_alignment) independently flagged this inconsistency. The test for AC7 only required the reason to contain 'parse error', so the missing suffix passed all automated gates while producing divergent audit log data.

title: Do not add exported fields or methods without a production caller in the same change
content: Before submitting any change that defines a new exported field or method: verify at least one production code path sets the field to a non-zero value or calls the method. If no caller exists, remove the field/method — do not leave it for future use. Empty files containing only a package declaration must not be committed. YAGNI applies to API surface.
rationale: Dead exported fields actively mislead: a reader seeing RefinementGuidance on a packet struct assumes refinement guidance flows into prompts — it does not. Five independent instances of dead API surface appeared in a single run, indicating this is a systematic gap, not a one-off. The rule is enforced at write time (executor self-check) rather than requiring a new validator.
